title: Quiz: ARMv8 Assembly - Intermediate
prompt: Work through argument registers, instruction aliases, the frame record, integer division, condition flags, and stepping in gdb.

questions.question: What role do registers x0 through x7 play in an AArch64 procedure call?
options: They are callee-saved registers.
They pass the first eight arguments into a procedure and carry the result back out.
They hold intra-procedure-call scratch data.
They act as the frame pointer and the procedure link register.
questions.explanation: The first eight arguments travel in x0 through x7, and the result comes back in x0. Anything past the eighth argument is passed on the stack instead.
questions.hint: Think about where arguments have to be sitting before you execute a bl.

questions.question: The instruction cmp x20, x21 is an alias. Which instruction does the assembler actually encode?
options: subs xzr, x20, x21
adds xzr, x20, x21
sub x20, x20, x21
ands xzr, x20, x21
questions.explanation: cmp subtracts with the s suffix so the condition flags are set, and writes the difference to xzr so the numeric result is thrown away. That is why cmp never disturbs either operand.
questions.hint: Comparing means subtracting and keeping the flags, not the difference.

questions.question: At the top of a routine, what does stp x29, x30, [sp, -16]! accomplish?
options: It loads 16 bytes from the stack into x29 and x30.
It subtracts 16 from sp first, then stores x29 and x30 into the 16 bytes it just allocated.
It sets sp to -16.
It stores x29 and x30, then adds 16 to sp to release the space.
questions.explanation: The ! makes this pre-indexed, so sp moves down by 16 before the store. Those 16 bytes hold the saved frame pointer and link register, and that pair is the frame record.
questions.hint: The ! decides whether sp moves before or after the store.

questions.question: What happens to the remainder when sdiv divides one register by another?
options: It is stored in x8, the indirect result register.
It raises an exception.
The quotient is truncated toward zero and the remainder is discarded.
It is written to the destination register alongside the quotient.
questions.explanation: sdiv produces only an integer quotient, truncated toward zero, and keeps nothing else. To recover the remainder you multiply the quotient back and subtract, which msub does in one instruction.
questions.hint: Divide 14 by 3 with sdiv and the destination register holds 4.

questions.question: In gdb, what is the difference between si and ni?
options: si steps over calls, ni steps into them.
Both execute one instruction, but at a bl the ni command runs the whole call and stops after it returns, while si stops on the callee's first instruction.
si prints signed integers, ni prints negative integers.
There is no difference; they are aliases for the same command.
questions.explanation: Both advance by one machine instruction, so on ordinary instructions they behave the same. They diverge only at a call: si steps into the callee, ni steps over it.
questions.hint: Read them as 'step instruction' and 'next instruction'.

questions.question: Which condition flag records that the result of an operation is negative?
options: Z
N
V
C
questions.explanation: The N flag takes the value of the result's sign bit, bit 63 for an X register and bit 31 for a W register. Most instructions leave the flags alone; the s-suffixed forms such as subs and adds, along with cmp, cmn, and tst, are the ones that write them.
questions.hint: One of the four flags copies the sign bit of the result.

questions.question: In GAS, which prefix marks an immediate written in binary?
options: 0x
a leading 0
0b
questions.explanation: 0b introduces a binary literal, so 0b101 is 5. A leading 0x means hexadecimal, a bare leading 0 means octal, and # is the optional immediate marker, not a radix.
questions.hint: Hex takes a letter after the zero, and so does binary.

questions.question: What does it mean that x19 through x28 are callee-saved?
options: Their values are wiped when a function returns.
A routine that wants to use one must save it on entry and restore it before returning, so a caller sees them unchanged across a call.
The hardware saves and restores them automatically on every bl.
They are scratch registers that nobody has to preserve.
questions.explanation: Callee-saved means the routine being called owns the responsibility: it puts the values back before returning. That is what lets a caller keep a value in x19 across a bl without spilling it.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the call, caller or callee, has to do the saving.
